statements.says: Studio draws a small symbol for four jobs, and the fourth alphabet, Order, says which way a sorted column runs.
The sort direction marks are ▲ and ▼, and they belong to Order.
A symbol still belongs to one alphabet, may be reused inside it, and the test that fails when a symbol crosses alphabets is unchanged.
Alphabet is a closed union, so the set of jobs is written in one place and a fifth needs a decision of its own.
The sort marks live with the table they serve and join the list the crossing test reads.
The Sessions table sorts on every column both ways, so a heading has to say which column was sorted and which way it ran.
None of the three existing jobs fits a sort mark, and putting it in one would give a reader a shape that means two things.
↑ was already Publish in the identity alphabet, so taking it for a sort direction would be the crossing the test catches.
A new alphabet should cost a paragraph, because the alternative is eight folders each inventing their own again.
Marking the sorted column with colour or weight alone was rejected, because a reader would not see which way it ran, and colour alone is the failure the alphabet rule opens with.
Writing the direction as a word in the heading was rejected, because a heading that grows moves the columns beside it every time a reader clicks.
Drawing a triangle in CSS instead of a character was rejected as a dodge, because a drawn mark is already treated as a symbol that answers to the alphabets.
Forcing the mark into the condition alphabet was rejected, because ascending is not a condition and a reader reads those shapes as how a part is doing.
It supersedes the part of the earlier alphabet record that names three jobs, and everything else that record decided stands.
